title: Magic in quantum trajectory unravelings of noisy random quantum circuits
authors: Sara Santos, Alessio Paviglianiti, Vincenzo Savona
abstract: The quantum-trajectory description of a noisy quantum circuit is not unique: every Kraus representation of the noise channel defines a different unraveling, i.e., a different ensemble of pure states that averages to the same density matrix. While all unravelings share the same expectation values of observables, they generally differ in the amount of quantum resources carried by the individual trajectories. Here we study non-stabilizerness, or magic, quantified by the stabilizer Rényi entropy, in quantum-trajectory unravelings of Haar-random and $T$-doped random Clifford brickwork circuits subject to local dephasing noise of strength $p$. The canonical unraveling in terms of Pauli jumps is Clifford and leaves magic untouched, so that trajectories retain the Haar-random value of non-stabilizerness. Exploring the full two-parameter family of minimal unravelings, we find that the trajectory-averaged magic can be substantially reduced by a state-independent choice of Kraus operators, and that the optimal choice is not in general the projective-measurement unraveling, but a two-outcome generalized measurement in which the Kraus operators correspond to a weak measurement of the noisy qubit. The optimal unraveling reduces the extensive magic density of the trajectories by a $p$-dependent factor without altering its linear scaling with system size. At the same time, it produces a very broad distribution of magic over trajectories, with a sizable fraction of trajectories retaining Haar-random magic. Since the cost of stabilizer-based classical simulation grows exponentially with the magic of the state, these high-magic trajectories, rather than the average, control the simulation cost. Our results delineate the potential and the limitations of unraveling optimization as a route to the classical simulation of noisy quantum dynamics with stabilizer methods.
summary: This paper investigates the non-uniqueness of quantum trajectories used to model noisy quantum circuits. By quantifying 'magic' using stabilizer entropy, the authors show that while the average magic can be reduced by choosing an optimal unraveling, the simulation cost is dictated by the few trajectories that retain high, near-maximal magic. This limits the effectiveness of stabilizer-based classical simulation methods.
main_problem: The quantum-trajectory description of noisy quantum circuits is non-unique, leading to different estimates of quantum resources like non-stabilizerness (magic).
main_result: The optimal unraveling, which is not the standard projective measurement, can substantially reduce the average magic, but the simulation cost is controlled by the high-magic trajectories, not the average.
method: The authors analyze the non-uniqueness of quantum unravelings by quantifying non-stabilizerness using the stabilizer Rényi entropy ($M_2$) for various noise models.
model_or_system: The study uses noisy random quantum circuits (Haar-random or T-doped Clifford) on $n$ qubits subjected to local dephasing noise ($p$).
key_observables: Non-stabilizerness (Magic), quantified by the stabilizer Rényi entropy ($M_2$), and the trajectory-averaged magic.
important_parameters: Noise strength ($p$), system size ($n$), and the choice of unraveling parameters ($	heta, \phi$).
main_assumptions: The simulation cost of stabilizer-based classical methods grows exponentially with the magic of the state.
figures_summary: Figures compare the evolution of magic ($M_2$) for different unravelings (canonical vs. optimal) under noise, showing how the average magic changes while high-magic trajectories persist.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the magic calculated using different Kraus representations (unravelings) for various noise types (dephasing, depolarizing, amplitude damping), establishing which unraveling yields the minimum average magic.
why_interesting: It provides a deep theoretical understanding of how noise modeling choices (unravelings) impact the quantifiable resources (magic) used in quantum simulation, which is crucial for understanding the limits of classical simulation.

The vertical dashed lines delimit com- plete brickwork layers, each formed by two sublayers acting on complementary sets of nearest-neighbor bonds. (a) Haar- random circuit, in which each green block is an independently sampled two-qubit Haar unitary. (b) T-doped Clifford circuit, in which each blue block is an independently sampled two- qubit Clifford and a T gate is applied independently to each participating qubit with probability q. Red circles denote the local single-qubit noise channel applied after each ideal gate block.

Each curve averages over 80 random circuit realizations, with 1000 trajectories per re- alization.

Each panel compares the canonical unraveling (θ = 0) with the quantum-jump unravel- ing (θ = θ∗), with ϕ = 0 in both cases. Circuits contain n = 8 qubits and 32 layers. FIG. 4. Magic in noisy Haar-random brickwork circuits as a function of the unraveling parameters. (a)–(c) M 2/M H 2 at the end of circuits with n = 8 qubits and NL = 16 layers, for dephasing probabilities p = 0.01 in (a),(d), p = 0.05 in (b),(e), and p = 0.1 in (c),(f).
